transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-06-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 1h12m (72 minutes)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Li (Redwood SE), David Ruiz (Cypress Head of ML), Priya Shah (Platform Eng), Emma Tanner (SRE), Noah Bennett (Product)

Summary:
Quick scoping session to align on latency SLO framing (TTFT vs TPOT), target percentiles, workload sizing, and a measurement plan for the POC. Customer wants deterministic first-token latency for interactive flows but also needs cost/per-token visibility for high-throughput batch scoring. Agree to run a lab benchmark with replayed traffic plus synthetic amplification, compare hosted vs dedicated profiles, and define pass/fail acceptance criteria.

Topics covered:
- Definitions: TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (time-per-token / per-token throughput metrics)
- Percentiles to measure: p50, p95, p99 and guidance on which to use for acceptance
- Workload shape: interactive chat (short prompts), document summarization (long sequences), batch embedding/score jobs
- Warm vs cold KV/prefix cache effects and how to measure them
- Measurement plan: traffic replay, synthetic load generator, warmup windows, sample sizes
- Acceptance criteria draft and fallback policies (model variants, quantized builds)

Action items and links referenced in call:
- Redwood to upload benchmark harness repo link (placeholder: https://redwood.internal/bench/harness)
- Customer to provide sanitized traffic sketch + 200 example requests (CSV or JSONL)
- Security docs: Redwood SOC2 + encryption notes (Jordan will attach)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Okay, thanks everyone for joining. We, uh, wanted to keep this tight — 60-ish minutes — and walk through how we should define the TTFT vs TPOT SLOs for your POC, plus what we need to run the benchmarks.
[00:18] David (Customer): Yeah thanks. Our main user story is interactive chat for support agents. We need first token to be snappy, like under, you know, we think 300 to 400 ms at p95, but we want to validate. We also have a high-volume daily scoring pipeline that is cost sensitive.
[00:35] Maya (SE): Great. Quick definitions so we're aligned — TTFT is time from request arrival to the first token emitted; TPOT in our discussion we mean the per-token tail behavior or effective tokens-per-second once streaming starts. Sometimes teams call it per-token latency or tpot shorthand.
[00:50] Priya (Customer): Sorry to interrupt, do you include queueing time in TTFT? Our infra often puts requests behind an ingress LB and tokenization step.
[00:59] Maya (SE): Good question. For the POC measurements we recommend measuring at the Redwood SDK boundary — after your tokenization / enrichment step — so queueing upstream is excluded. But we'll record end-to-end as an auxiliary metric.
[01:12] Emma (SRE): Also want to capture cold start behavior — if we route traffic to Dedicated that has scaled down, TTFT could spike. How do you suggest we measure that?
[01:21] Jordan (AE): We'll do two modes: steady-state warm benchmark and cold-start sweep. Warm benchmark will have a 10 minute warmup window to populate KV/prefix caches; cold will intentionally scale-to-zero then re-hydrate. We'll report both.
[01:33] Noah (Product): From a product POV, our acceptance should be based on steady-state TTFT p95 and also a 99th percentile guardrail for peaks. For batch scoring we care about TPOT and overall cost per 1M tokens.
[01:45] David: For numbers, we're thinking p95 TTFT < 350ms and p99 < 700ms as a starting hypothesis. For TPOT maybe p50 ~ 5-8ms/token and p95 < 20ms/token on the models we plan to serve. But that's just a gut check.
[02:00] Maya: Those are reasonable for the medium-sized open models. We'll need to know your average prompt length and response length — both for chat and summarization — to size throughput.
[02:10] David: Average user prompt is 18 tokens, responses average 64 tokens in chat. Summaries go up to 1,200 tokens. Batch scoring job is 100k requests/day, each scoring call does a 512-token forward pass.
[02:23] Maya: Perfect. For the benchmark we'll synthesize three traffic profiles: interactive chat (short), long-form summarization (long), and batch scoring (throughput). We'll run each under progressive load ramps and measure TTFT and token throughput.
[02:36] Priya: About sampling — how many samples do you need to be statistically confident at p99? We don't want the bench to be flaky.
[02:44] Maya: We'll aim for at least 10k observed requests per traffic class for p99 stability in steady-state, but for the long summaries it's slower so we'll run longer windows. Also run multiple repeats.
[02:56] Emma: Can you outline the warmup procedure so we know how to replicate in our environment?
[03:01] Maya: Sure — 10 minutes of sustained requests at 50% of target QPS, then a 5 minute ramp to target. For p99 we recommend collecting at least 30 minutes at target after ramp. We'll provide the exact script.
[03:14] Jordan: On acceptance criteria, here's a draft matrix I want to confirm with you: for interactive chat steady-state, TTFT p95 <= 350ms AND TTFT p99 <= 700ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token. For long-form summarization, TTFT p95 <= 800ms because of longer context and memory effects. For batch scoring, we'll use TPOT average and a cost threshold of $X per 1M tokens — we'll calculate once we know model variant.
[03:36] David: That sounds reasonable. On cost thresholds — is that cost to Redwood hosted or our projected cost on Dedicated? We might want both.
[03:43] Jordan: We can produce unit cost for both hosted and dedicated profiles. The bench will measure tokens and GPU utilization; we'll produce projected unit economics for the pilot traffic.
[03:52] Priya: Let's talk about cache effects — KV cache and prefix cache can change TTFT a lot. How will you control for that?
[03:59] Maya: We'll run with cache enabled (realistic) and disabled (cold path) and report both. For prefix caching we'll instrument hits/misses and show how p95 shifts with hit-rate. We also plan a short experiment to seed caches with a popular set of prefixes to emulate production.
[04:14] Emma: Security — we need to ensure the traces are sanitized. Anything Redwood needs for SOC2 / encryption?
[04:20] Jordan: We'll attach our SOC2 summary and KMS notes. For the POC traces we only need anonymized text; if PII is present, we can redact with a simple script. We'll provide a template.
[04:32] David: On model variants — we want to test: 1) the base open model, 2) a quantized int8 variant, and 3) a distilled/lite variant. Do you support automatic fallback between variants?
[04:43] Maya: Yes, the runtime supports variant routing and fallbacks. For the POC we'll run the three variants in separate bench runs and then one mixed run to emulate routing policy. We'll observe differences in TTFT & TPOT and quantify quality regressions if any (we'll produce a small eval set).
[04:59] Noah: How do we measure quality regressions automatically? We need a simple metric to combine with latency for acceptance.
[05:05] Maya: We'll run a small prompt set — we'll use ROUGE/L or a semantic similarity score (emb cosine) for chat replies. The POC acceptance can require quality within X% of baseline. We'll propose thresholds in the draft SLO matrix.
[05:18] Jordan: For sampling plan and measurement windows — here's the proposal: collect at least 10k chat requests for steady-state p99; 5 repeats of the long summary run to get stable percentiles; batch scoring measured by sustained throughput to reach cost estimates. We'll also do a 24-hour soak at low QPS to catch rare jitter.
[05:36] Priya: For the 24-hour soak, can we run that in our VPC private deployment? We have concerns about sending traces externally.
[05:44] Jordan: Absolutely. We can run the Redwood Private image in your VPC — the bench harness supports on-prem runners. We'll need a network endpoint and service account. We'll coordinate security steps.
[05:56] Emma: Also want to capture metrics at infra level: GPU utilization, CPU steal, memory for kv cache. Do you export those?
[06:03] Maya: Yes, we'll capture GPU utilization and a token-per-second derived metric plus queue depth. We'll provide Grafana dashboards and OTLP metrics.
[06:12] David: A slightly related question — if we see TTFT spikes caused by a bad tokenization step upstream, how will we correlate and debug?
[06:19] Maya: We'll instrument request traces and return a unique request id so you can correlate logs from your tokenization pipeline. For the bench we can simulate upstream latency as part of the test.
[06:29] Jordan: Ok, moving towards timeline: Jordan to share draft SLO matrix by 2027-06-17, Maya uploads harness by 6/18, customer sends traces by 6/20, bench runs week of 6/28, results review 7/2. Does everyone agree?
[06:44] David: Yes. One ask — please include cold-path p99 as a separate column in the matrix. That will be important for SLA negotiations.
[06:52] Maya: Noted. We'll include cold and warm columns.
[06:55] Noah: For pass/fail, do we want a strict threshold or a graded system (e.g., green/yellow/red)?
[07:01] Jordan: Recommend graded: green meets all steady-state targets; yellow meets p95 but marginal for p99 or cold; red fails either steady-state p95 or quality threshold. We'll map next actions for each bucket.
[07:12] Emma: Anything else on instrumentation? We want request-level percentiles and also microsecond-level histograms for TTFT to spot long tails.
[07:20] Maya: We'll produce HdrHistogram outputs and raw CSVs so you can re-run percentile computations.
[07:27] David: Great. If the bench shows we meet TTFT but cost is high, can Redwood recommend batching / quantization knobs?
[07:34] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Optimize will provide quantization and batching recommendations and we'll simulate impact in the bench. We'll show unit economics before/after.
[07:44] Priya: Last operational question — what telemetry retention do you need for the POC? We're concerned about log volumes.
[07:50] Maya: For the POC we keep 30 days by default; we can shorten to 7 days for the bench artifacts and export compressed summaries to your S3.
[07:58] Jordan: Ok let's recap next steps and owners verbally quickly.
[08:02] Jordan (AE): Jordan will send the SLO matrix draft and SOC2 + security pointer. Maya will upload bench harness and a traffic simulator config. David will send anonymized traces. Emma will confirm security requirements. Schedule bench run for week of 6/28 and review 7/2.
[08:18] David: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:22] Noah: Thanks, bye.
[08:24] [call ended]
